subtype: Friend × Taking sides in a conflict [Actor]
passage:
Pranav: You saw what Neha posted about me. Whose side are you on?
Ishita: I saw it. Posting it in the group was unkind.
Pranav: So you agree with me!
Ishita: Not fully. Dropping out of Neha's birthday plan without telling anyone wasn't fair either.
Pranav: Wow. So you're on her side.
Ishita: I'm not on a side. I told Neha the same thing this morning. You both did something that hurt the other.
Pranav: That's not helping 😠
Ishita: I know it's annoying to hear. I'm still here, and I'll help you write her an honest message if you want.
Pranav: ...let me think.
Ishita: Take your time 🙂

qa.q: What did Ishita say she had told Neha that morning?
qa.a: The same thing she was telling Pranav: that both had done something that hurt the other.

qa.q: What is Pranav feeling in this chat, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Angry and frustrated. Pranav wants Ishita to agree and answers "That's not helping" with an angry face.

qa.q: How does Ishita say what she thinks is right without hurting either friend?
qa.a: She names what was unkind on both sides, offers to help with an honest message, and says she is still there.

qa.q: How might Neha see Ishita's stance?
qa.a: Neha may be relieved that Ishita is not attacking behind Neha's back, or a little stung to hear their own part named.

grounding: Ishita is pressed to choose sides and states what she thinks is right about both without gossiping to either.

subtype: Friend × Taking sides in a conflict [Actor]
passage:
Last term, Shankar and Gauri both came to me on the same evening, about the same thing: who deserved the lead name on our robotics poster. Shankar texted, "You saw who stayed till midnight. Back me up." Gauri called: "You know the design was mine."
I'll be honest: my first move was the cowardly one. I told Shankar, "Yeah, you did more," and then told Gauri, "Obviously it was your design." Both of them felt sure I was on their side.
Then the three of us ended up in the lab together, and I realised it would all come out. So I said it plainly, to both at once: "I think the design was Gauri's and the build was Shankar's. I think you should both be named, in alphabetical order." Shankar sighed. Gauri rolled her eyes. Neither of them was happy.
But nobody felt lied to. That was the part I'd been missing.
— Aadhya

qa.q: What were Shankar and Gauri arguing over?
qa.a: Who deserved the lead name on the robotics poster.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya first agree with each of them separately?
qa.a: Aadhya felt anxious to be liked and to avoid conflict, which led to the cowardly move of telling both what they wanted to hear.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Aadhya, and why?
qa.a: Saying one honest view to both at once, design to Gauri and build to Shankar with both named; neither was pleased, but nobody felt lied to.

qa.q: How might Gauri have felt on learning about the first message to Shankar?
qa.a: Betrayed and misled, since Gauri had been told the opposite.

grounding: Shows being pressed to take sides, the pitfall of telling each side what they want, and then stating one honest view to both.

subtype: Friend × Taking sides in a conflict [Actor]
passage:
Supervisor's note, customer support floor, Thursday
There has been friction between Manjula and Dinesh over last week's shift swap, and both have been trying to recruit Pankaj, who sits between them. Today at lunch I saw it come to a head. Manjula said loudly, "Pankaj, tell him he's being selfish."
Pankaj put down his spoon. He said, "I think Dinesh should have asked before swapping. I also think it's unfair to call him selfish in front of everyone. I'm not going to carry messages between you two." Then he went back to eating.
Both looked annoyed. But later, Dinesh apologised to Manjula for the swap, and Manjula said she had been harsh. I noticed Pankaj didn't repeat either side's comments to the other all afternoon.
I have scheduled a short meeting on Monday to set a clear swap process, and I will thank Pankaj privately for keeping things calm.

qa.q: What was the friction between Manjula and Dinesh about?
What did Pankaj's putting down his spoon suggest?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable at being pulled in, but calm and determined to answer honestly rather than pick a side.

qa.q: What did the supervisor plan after the lunch?
qa.a: A short meeting on Monday to set a clear swap process, and a private thank-you to Pankaj.

qa.q: How did Manjula respond to Pankaj's answer?
qa.a: Annoyed at first, but later she admitted she had been harsh.

grounding: Illustrates being pressed to choose between two colleagues and stating what one thinks is right without hurting either or carrying tales.
